decisions.quote:
We have two main results. 1) Gaps between elite and mass decision-making are larger in studies
whose manipulations appear to have worked. Only a small number of the these 162 treatments
significantly affected masses (N=28) or elites (N=30). This low rate suggests the possibility that
almost all of these experiments failed to successfully manipulate either masses or elites. If so, we
may not be able to conclude that masses and elites respond similarly to experiments with confidence
until political scientists produce more experiments with actual treatment effects or with successful
manipulation checks in cases of null effects.
decisions.reason: The shipped quote reflects only the intermediate summary of the first two checks (study inclusion criteria and treatment pooling) halfway through Section 3.1. Across the full pre-registered robustness and heterogeneity re-analyses of Claim 1, the authors find that when restricting to studies with significant mass or elite treatment effects (successful manipulations), the rate of statistically significant mass-elite differences rises from 12% to 43%-63% after FDR adjustment (vs. 7% when neither is significant). In both the Abstract and the Conclusion, the authors explicitly judge that these re-analyses materially qualify Kertzer's central inference that masses and elites respond similarly to experiments, fitting 'robustness challenges'.
